title: Decision trees
story:
Every method up to here fits one formula to the whole input space. That is a strong commitment: it says the same functional form governs the cheap cases and the expensive ones, the young customers and the old ones, the ordinary days and the holidays. A tree makes the opposite commitment. It does not fit the space, it cuts it.

The procedure is recursive partitioning. At a node, consider every variable and every threshold, pick the single test that best separates the observations by some impurity criterion, split the data in two, and do it again on each part. Keep going until a stopping rule fires. Each leaf then predicts one constant — a class, or an average — for everything that reaches it.

Three consequences follow immediately from that description, and they are why the method behaves so differently from the rest of this track. Because each test involves one variable at a time, the boundaries are axis-aligned: the model can carve out rectangles but must approximate a diagonal with a staircase. Because the test asks only whether a value is above or below a threshold, the rule depends on the order of values within a variable and not on their scale, which is exactly why scaling a feature leaves a tree's predictions untouched. And because a leaf predicts a constant, a tree cannot extrapolate — feed it an input beyond anything it saw and it returns the value of whichever region it lands in, unchanged.

The standard treatment is the 1984 monograph by Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone, and one of its remarks is worth keeping: this use of trees was unthinkable before computers. The method is not clever mathematics, it is exhaustive search made cheap, and it arrived when searching every variable and every threshold at every node became affordable.

The limitation that matters is in the word best. Finding the optimal tree — the one with the lowest error over all possible trees of a given size — is intractable, so every practical algorithm is greedy: it takes the locally best split and never reconsiders. That is usually fine and occasionally fatal. A relationship where neither variable is informative alone but their combination is fully determining will show no good first split at all, because the criterion evaluates each variable in isolation. The tree cannot see a structure it has to make two moves to reach.

problem.name: Recursive partitioning
problem.shape: Different regions of the input space behave differently, and a single global formula has to cover all of them at once.
tell: the relationship changes character in different parts of the range
features are on wildly different scales and nobody wants to normalise
the model has to be explainable as a sequence of conditions
interactions matter more than individual effects
problem.move: Split recursively on one variable at a time, choosing the test that best separates by an impurity criterion, and let each leaf predict a constant. Control depth or leaf size deliberately, since an unconstrained tree will isolate individual observations, and check whether the structure you care about is visible to a single split before trusting the result.
problem.invariant: Each test involves one variable and a threshold, so regions are axis-aligned and predictions depend only on the order of values within a variable, never on their scale.
problem.breaks: The greedy construction evaluates each variable in isolation at each node, so a relationship in which no single variable is informative alone — but a pair is jointly determining — presents no good first split and will be missed entirely. Optimal trees are intractable to find, so this is a property of every practical implementation rather than of one.

cost.time: every variable and every candidate threshold is examined at every node, which is why the method waited for computers
cost.space: the tree itself, which grows with the number of leaves and is readable while it stays small
cost.beats: one global formula, which cannot change character across the space, and distance-based methods, which need the scaling this does not

worked.problem: Why are the splits chosen greedily, and what does that cost?
worked.reasoning:
Because finding the best tree is intractable, and the cost is that any structure requiring two moves to reach is invisible.

Take the intractability first. A tree is a sequence of choices, and each choice changes what the subsequent choices are selecting among. Searching all trees of a given size means searching a space that grows combinatorially in the number of variables, thresholds and depths, and the problem of finding an optimal tree is not one anybody solves exactly at realistic scale. So every practical algorithm takes the locally best split by an impurity criterion and never revisits it.

Usually this is fine, because usually there is a variable that is informative on its own, and taking it first does not preclude finding the rest of the structure below. The greedy path and a good path coincide often enough that the method works.

The failure case is specific and worth being able to name. Consider a target determined by whether two binary variables agree — informative when taken together, and each one individually telling you nothing, since for either variable alone both outcomes remain equally likely. Evaluated at the root, every variable scores zero improvement. The criterion sees nothing to split on, and depending on the stopping rule the tree either terminates immediately or splits arbitrarily. The structure is fully determining and completely invisible to a procedure that scores variables one at a time.

There is a second, subtler cost. Greedy construction makes the tree unstable: because a split near the root determines the entire subtree beneath it, a small change in the data that flips an early split produces a completely different tree. That instability is not a bug to be fixed within a single tree — it is the property the next two lessons exploit, by growing many trees deliberately made to disagree and combining them.

What I would do about it in practice is less exotic than it sounds. Give the tree the interaction directly as an engineered feature if you suspect one. Allow enough depth that a split with no immediate payoff can still be taken. And check whether an ensemble of trees finds structure the single tree missed, since the randomisation there sometimes reaches what greedy search alone will not.

problem.practice: Build a target that depends on whether two binary features agree, fit a shallow tree, and look at what it chooses at the root. Then add the interaction as an explicit feature and fit again. Separately, scale one feature by a factor of a thousand and confirm the tree's predictions do not move.

beats.broke: A single global formula has to describe the entire input space, forcing one functional form onto regions that may behave nothing like each other.
beats.fix: Cut the space rather than fitting it — choose one variable and one threshold at a time, split, recurse, and let every region carry its own constant prediction.
beats.cost: Each choice is locally best rather than globally best, because finding the optimal tree is intractable — so a split that only pays off in combination with a later one is never found.

interview.q: Why are the splits chosen greedily, and what does that cost?
interview.trap: Treating greediness as an implementation shortcut that a better library might avoid. Optimal trees are intractable, so it is a property of the method — and the cost is specific: any structure where no single variable is informative alone is invisible at the root.

takeaway: A tree cuts the space instead of fitting it, so it ignores scaling and cannot extrapolate — and because the split at each node is locally best and never reconsidered, a relationship where no single variable is informative alone is invisible at the root.
